issues.legal_issue: An appointment of a guardian and mortgage sanctions covering properties are not limited to the guardian’s claimed share when the orders impose no such limitation.
material_facts: The guardian’s appointment order declared her guardian of the minor’s person and property and did not limit the appointment to a half share.
The orders granting permission to mortgage referred to the properties as a whole, and the court’s reasons described them as the minor’s properties.
The guardian’s applications stated that she claimed one half of the properties and the minor owned the other half.
issues.conclusion: The appointment and mortgage sanctions were not limited to the minor’s half share; as to their scope, they covered the properties and authorized a mortgage over the entire interest in them.
issues.legal_principle: The scope of the guardian’s appointment and authority is determined from the relevant orders read together. An order appointing a guardian of the minor’s property, without a stated limitation, does not itself establish that the appointment is confined to the minor’s share as described in the application. The Court referred to In the matter of Sirsh Chander Singh and Others in explaining that whether a person was appointed guardian of property is determined from the appointment instrument as a whole.

predicates.appeal_over_extent_of_guardian_mortgage: A party in an appeal disputes whether a guardian’s mortgage authority extended beyond the minor’s claimed share.
predicates.guardian_appointment_unlimited: The court’s appointment order made the person guardian of the minor’s property without limiting the appointment to a particular share.
predicates.mortgage_sanction_covers_properties_as_a: The court’s mortgage permission referred to the properties as a whole rather than to a specified share.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns the extent of a guardian’s mortgage authority, an unrestricted appointment and permission covering the properties as a whole mean that the authority is not limited to the guardian’s claimed share.

issues.legal_issue: Mortgage sanctions do not bind a minor’s estate when a guardian appointed under a will conceals restrictions on alienation and the court does not expressly remove those restrictions.
material_facts: The will appointed the widow executor and guardian and bequeathed the properties to the minor son, while placing restrictions on the widow’s power to alienate them.
The widow applied for appointment and mortgage permission without disclosing the will or its restrictions.
The mortgage permission was sought under the statutory procedure for guardians appointed by the court, and the court did not make a written order removing the restrictions imposed by the will.
issues.conclusion: The mortgage sanctions were invalid and could not bind the minor’s estate because the will and its restrictions were not disclosed and the court did not expressly authorize alienation notwithstanding those restrictions.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 28 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, a guardian appointed by will may dispose of the ward’s immovable property notwithstanding restrictions in the instrument only if the court, after being apprised of them, permits the disposal by written order. Sections 29 and 31(2) do not provide the applicable permission procedure for a guardian appointed by will, because section 29 concerns a guardian appointed or declared by the court. Section 30 makes a disposal contrary to the applicable restrictions voidable. The Court also relied on In the matter of Sirsh Chander Singh and Others in determining from the will that the widow was guardian of the minor’s property.

rule.if: minor_estate_mortgage_dispute and guardian_appointed_by_will and will_restricts_alienation and restrictions_not_disclosed_to_court and no_written_order_overrides_restrictions

predicates.minor_estate_mortgage_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a mortgage of a minor’s property binds the minor’s estate.
predicates.guardian_appointed_by_will: The instrument appointing the guardian was a will.
predicates.will_restricts_alienation: The will limited the guardian’s power to alienate the minor’s immovable property.
predicates.restrictions_not_disclosed_to_court: The guardian sought permission to mortgage without telling the court about the will’s restrictions.
predicates.no_written_order_overrides_restrictions: The court did not make a written order expressly permitting the alienation notwithstanding the restrictions.

issues.definition: In a dispute over a minor’s mortgaged property, a will-appointed guardian’s undisclosed alienation restrictions, not expressly overridden in writing by the court, mean that the sanction does not bind the minor’s estate.

issues.legal_issue: A respondent may rely on the invalidity of a voidable mortgage sanction as a defence to an appellant’s claim for greater recovery without first bringing a separate suit, subject to restitution.
material_facts: The respondents did not appeal the part of the decree that already allowed recovery from one half of the mortgaged properties.
The appellants sought in the appeal to extend recovery to the entire interest in the properties, relying on the mortgage sanctions.
The respondents challenged the validity of those sanctions in defence, and the benefits received were available for restitution, including sale proceeds retained by the estate administrator.
issues.conclusion: The respondents could avoid the sanctions in defence, without a separate suit, to resist the appellants’ claim for greater recovery, provided restitution was made.
issues.legal_principle: A respondent who does not appeal may support the decree already in their favour on a ground decided against them, without thereby attacking that decree. A voidable disposal under section 30 may be challenged in defence without a separate suit, but restitution of the benefits received is a just condition of avoiding it. The Court relied on Parshotam Das v. Nazir Husain, Peria Karuppan Chetty v. Kandasamy Chetty, and Abbas Hussain v. Kiran Shashi Devi for the restitution principle, and on the Madras High Court’s decision in Venkata Rao v. Satyanarayanamurthy concerning a respondent’s ability to support a decree without cross-appealing.

rule.if: appeal_seeking_greater_recovery and respondent_supports_existing_decree and respondent_challenges_voidable_sanction_defensively and restitution_of_benefits_is_provided

predicates.appeal_seeking_greater_recovery: An appellant asks the appellate court to extend recovery beyond what the existing decree awarded.
predicates.respondent_supports_existing_decree: The respondent seeks to preserve the part of the decree already in the respondent’s favour rather than set it aside.
predicates.respondent_challenges_voidable_sanction_: The respondent relies on the invalidity of a voidable sanction only to resist the appellant’s additional claim.
predicates.restitution_of_benefits_is_provided: The benefit received through the challenged transaction is restored or made available for restoration.

issues.definition: When an appellant seeks greater recovery, a respondent preserving an existing favourable decree may resist the additional claim by challenging a voidable sanction without a separate suit if the benefit received is restored.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may frame relief that gives effect to restitution and the justice of the case when an invalid voidable sanction underlay the decree and the appellant seeks a wider recovery.
material_facts: The appellants advanced the mortgage money in good faith on the strength of the court’s sanctions, and there was no finding that the transactions lacked necessity.
The High Court had granted recovery on the basis that the sanctions were valid, but the sanctions were found invalid because the will and its restrictions had been concealed.
One property had been sold with court approval, and its proceeds were retained by the estate administrator; another property remained subject to the mortgage claim.
The respondents were entitled to avoid the sanctions in defence on condition of restitution.
issues.conclusion: Applying Order 41, rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court set aside the High Court’s decree and directed payment of the mortgage principal with interest, secured by the retained sale proceeds and the entire interest in the other mortgaged property.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41, rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers an appellate court to pass the decree or order that ought to have been passed and any further or other decree required by justice. Where a voidable disposal is avoided, restitution is a proper condition; the Court applied the restitution principle recognized in Parshotam Das v. Nazir Husain, Peria Karuppan Chetty v. Kandasamy Chetty, and Abbas Hussain v. Kiran Shashi Devi.

rule.if: appeal_seeking_greater_mortgage_recovery and original_decree_rests_on_sanction_found_invalid and lender_advanced_money_in_good_faith and no_finding_of_absent_necessity and benefits_available_for_restitution

predicates.appeal_seeking_greater_mortgage_recovery: A creditor appeals seeking recovery beyond the amount or property covered by the existing decree.
predicates.original_decree_rests_on_sanction_found_: The decree under appeal granted recovery on the basis of a sanction that the appellate court finds invalid.
predicates.lender_advanced_money_in_good_faith: The creditor advanced the money honestly in reliance on the court’s sanction.
predicates.no_finding_of_absent_necessity: The court has not found that the transaction lacked necessity or benefit for the minor.
predicates.benefits_available_for_restitution: The benefit received through the transaction, such as retained sale proceeds, remains available to be restored.

issues.definition: Where an appeal seeks greater mortgage recovery from a decree based on an invalid sanction, good-faith lending, no finding of absent necessity, and available benefits for restoration may justify an appellate order securing recovery against available property on a restitutionary basis.
